claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by nanoscale fluctuations in chemical ordering.
Chemical-ordering fluctuations create spatially varying energy barriers to melting.
Regions with enhanced local chemical order begin melting later than less-ordered regions.
The nanoparticles are initially solid and single phase.
The initial nanoparticles are macroscopically homogeneous solid solutions.
The initial nanoparticles may contain nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
A sub-melting anneal can enhance local chemical ordering in these nanoparticles.
A controlled sub-melting treatment can alternatively disrupt local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering changes interatomic bonding energies.
The bonding-energy changes associated with local order raise the melting barrier in ordered regions.
Ordering-enhanced annealed nanoparticles will have a higher premelting-onset temperature than as-synthesized nanoparticles.
Ordering-enhanced annealed nanoparticles will have a higher melting-onset temperature than as-synthesized nanoparticles.
The predicted onset-temperature increases will appear as shifts in DSC thermograms.
In situ electron microscopy can confirm the predicted difference in melting behavior.
The as-synthesized baseline particles have a random solid-solution atomic arrangement.
The proposed mechanism applies across the premelting and melting regimes of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles under inert, non-oxidizing conditions.
Surface curvature and particle-size distribution may govern the thermal response more strongly than chemical ordering.
Atomic-scale EDS compositional mapping can assess local chemical ordering.
